short: A factor that adjusts an index price for a corporate action while preserving the event's intended value.
long: PAF means Price Adjustment Factor. It scales the price used by a price index so an eligible corporate action does not create a false index move. For a cash distribution, the cited MSCI treatment uses PAF = (CumPx − Div) / CumPx: CumPx is the security price before it trades ex-distribution, and Div is the distribution amount. A PAF of none means no price adjustment is applied.

short: The theoretical ex-rights price: the blended price implied by the old shares and discounted new rights shares.
long: TERP means Theoretical Ex-Rights Price. It estimates the per-share price after a rights issue by combining the value of the existing shares with the subscription price and the new-share ratio. Index providers use it when eligible, usually in the price adjustment factor for in-the-money rights; the exact formula can vary with the rights terms and vendor methodology.

short: Number of shares outstanding; vendors use it as the share-count base for some materiality tests.
long: NOS means Number of Shares Outstanding. In the treatment text it is the pre-event or post-event share-count base used to measure whether an issuance or other share change is large enough for an index adjustment.

short: A factor representing the proportion of a company's shares available to foreign investors.
long: FIF means Foreign Inclusion Factor. It represents the portion of a company's shares that an index can include for foreign-investor access, after relevant ownership restrictions. In the cited rights-issue treatment, FIF changes are assessed alongside NOS and DIF changes; the dataset does not specify a separate FIF calculation here.

short: A factor representing the domestic-investor inclusion adjustment used in the cited MSCI share-change treatment.
long: DIF is the Domestic Inclusion Factor in the cited MSCI rights-issue treatment. It is listed with NOS and FIF as a share or investability measure whose change can be tested against cap-tier thresholds. The supplied treatment text does not define a separate DIF formula, so this guide does not infer one.

short: An index that tracks constituent price changes without reinvesting dividends or other cash distributions.
long: A Price Return Index measures the price movement of its constituents. Ordinary dividends are not reinvested into it; the market's ex-date price change is therefore treated according to the vendor's price-index rules. It is commonly abbreviated PR.

short: An index that tracks price changes plus the reinvestment of gross dividends or distributions.
long: A Total Return Index measures constituent price movement plus gross cash dividends reinvested on the applicable ex-date. It is commonly abbreviated TR. The reinvestment assumption makes it different from a Price Return Index even when both use the same constituents.

short: An index that tracks price changes plus dividends reinvested after the assumed withholding tax.
long: A Net Total Return Index measures constituent price movement plus dividends reinvested net of the assumed withholding tax. It is commonly abbreviated NTR or, in some treatment text, NR. This gives a more investor-realistic dividend return than a gross Total Return Index.

short: For a rights issue, the subscription price is below the relevant market price, giving the right positive value.
long: For a rights issue, in-the-money means the subscription price is below the relevant market price. The right has positive economic value, so methodologies commonly calculate a theoretical ex-rights price and apply a price adjustment, subject to the vendor's stated rules.

short: For a rights issue, the subscription price is at or above the relevant market price, so the right has no positive value.
long: For a rights issue, out-of-the-money means the subscription price is greater than or equal to the relevant market price. The right has zero or negative value; the cited treatments generally apply no price adjustment, though later share handling can still follow the vendor's rules.

short: A rule that compares a dividend with market price, often 5%, to decide whether the distribution is special and price-adjusted.
long: The dividend-size threshold mechanic compares the dividend amount with the security's market price. In the cited MSCI rule, a dividend at or above 5% of market price is classified as special and receives a Price Return adjustment; below 5% it is treated as ordinary with no Price Return adjustment. Total Return and Net Total Return reinvestment is separate from this Price Return classification.
